2    Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, POSITION AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

3    A.    My name is Lynn M. Ferry-Nelson, and I am the Vice President of Regulatory Affairs

16         for regulatory interactions, monitoring of regulatory filings, participation in

18         requirements.

22         Business Administration in Finance. I also earned my Project Manager Certification

23         from the University of California at Irvine. I have more than 30 years of utility,

19   Q.    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY IN THIS

20         PROCEEDING?

22         docket, including the direct testimonies of the Texas Industrial Energy Consumers

  1         (TIEC) and Cities Advocating Reasonable Deregulation (CARD) filed on July 1, 2026,

 2         and the direct testimony of the Commission Staff (Staff) filed on July 10, 2026.

 3         Company witness Alex E. Vaughan is also filing rebuttal testimony in this docket to

 4         address certain recommendations of the other parties in this proceeding. Attached to

 5         my rebuttal testimony as Exhibit LFN-1R is a revised copy of the proposed Contract

 6         for Electric Service Texas – Large Load (ES-LL Contract), which I support as

 7         reasonable, necessary, and in the best interests of the Company’s existing customers,

 9   Q.    IS THE COMPANY MODIFYING ANY OF THE TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF

10         THE PROPOSED ES-LL CONTRACT IN RESPONSE TO TESTIMONY FILED BY

11         STAFF, TIEC, AND CARD?

12   A.    Yes. As discussed in more detail below, the Company has revised the “Applicability”

13         section and has revised the “Ramp Period” section to clarify that this period may not

14         exceed five years. Finally, SWEPCO recommends that the “Initial Contract Term” be

15         revised to extend the term to 17 years, including the ramp period. As discussed below,

16         this change ensures that new large load customers will be billed for their firm contract

17         capacity for a minimum of 17 years, whether the Ramp Period is one year, three years,

18         or the full five years allowed under the proposed Contract.

19   Q.    PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS IN THIS PROCEEDING.

20   A.    I recommend that the Commission approve SWEPCO’s proposed ES-LL Contract, as

21         revised, as soon as practicable to ensure the prescribed protections for the Company

22         and its existing customers are in place prior to prospective large loads taking service

23         and ramping up to full operations in SWEPCO’s Texas service territory. The Company

                                                                                                      5
  1         seeks a constructive outcome in this docket that addresses the primary concerns of all

 2         parties and other stakeholders through the creation of a standardized service framework

 3         that fosters economic growth through certainty, and, most importantly, provides

 4         meaningful protections to the Company’s existing customer base. Sound and durable

 5         Commission policy in this area greatly reduces the risk of bringing large load customers

 6         online in the State of Texas, while ensuring the creditworthiness and long-term viability

 7         of the large load customers that ultimately do come online. As structured, the proposed

 8         ES-LL Contract includes widely used protections, including provisions that ensure

 9         long-term contracts and revenue streams cover costs imposed by these large loads, as

10         well as termination/exit fees and notice requirements that allow for a “bridge period”

11         during which newer and valuable capacity resources and other utility infrastructure can

12         be utilized to the benefit of different large load customers or the remaining customer

13         base through thoughtful, continuous capacity planning. Approved tariffs and form

14         contracts containing the key customer protections included in SWEPCO’s ES-LL

15         Contract have the added benefit of removing the more speculative data center projects

16         from the pipeline, thereby increasing the accuracy of the Company’s load forecasts and

17         associated capacity planning.


18                          III.    KEY CUSTOMER PROTECTIONS

19   Q.    STAFF, TIEC, AND CARD WITNESSES INSIST THAT THE COMMISSION’S

20         FOCUS WHEN CONSIDERING THE ES-LL CONTRACT SHOULD BE

21         PROTECTING EXISTING CUSTOMERS FROM COST SHIFTING. DO YOU

  1   A.    Absolutely. And to be clear, protecting customers goes hand in hand with protecting

 2         the Company from financial harm as well. SWEPCO agrees that the Commission’s

 3         central focus should be protecting the Company’s existing customers from

 4         inappropriate cost shifting, and the proposed ES-LL Contract accomplishes this goal.

 5         SWEPCO’s obligation is to serve all customers, including large load customers, and

 6         the Commission must also provide a workable path for new large load development to

 7         the benefit of the communities served by the Company in its Texas service territory.

 8         The risks and opportunities are real, with new large load customers having the ability

 9         to greatly expand the local tax base, create temporary and full-time jobs, contribute to

10         the effective utilization of existing and new infrastructure, and stabilize rates through

11         growth in billing units (sales). SWEPCO’s proposed ES-LL Contract minimizes the

12         risk and facilitates a path for serious projects committed to doing business in Texas for

13         many years.

18                 IV.     SPECIFIC CONTRACT TERMS AND CONDITIONS

19                                         A.    Applicability

20   Q.    TIEC      WITNESS           MCGLOTHLIN         RECOMMENDS             RAISING       THE

21         APPLICABILITY THRESHOLD FROM 75 MW TO 250 MW. WHAT IS YOUR

22         RESPONSE?



     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                       REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                         7                    LYNN M. FERRY-NELSON
                                                                                                        9
  1   A.      I disagree with Mr. McGlothlin’s proposed threshold and submit that a lower

 2           applicability threshold of 75 MW, consistent with other approved large load tariffs,

 3           offers greater protection to the Company and existing customers. For example:

 4                •   A 250 MW cutoff is too high and would leave a significant range of very large

 5                    loads outside the ES-LL Contract protections, increasing risks to existing

 6                    customers. Furthermore, the larger the threshold, the more opportunity for

 7                    customers to “game” the interconnection study and contract processes. For

 8                    example, a customer looking to add 500 MW of generation could submit two

 9                    study requests for 249.9 MW at two different but contiguous locations, using

10                    two different business names to avoid paying collateral, exit fees, and minimum

11                    bills.

12                •   The higher the threshold, the less protection is built in for other customers. A

13                    75 MW threshold is a reasonable trigger because it captures loads large enough

14                    to create material planning, resource, and cost-recovery risks.

15                •   As noted above, the 75 MW threshold is consistent with large load thresholds

16                    used or considered in other jurisdictions.

17                    Moreover, it appears that TIEC witness McGlothlin misapplied the findings of

18           the study he references. Based on my review, there is not one 500 MW load that is

19           included in the study, and Mr. McGlothlin may have inadvertently read the study results

20           of 0.5 MW as 0.5 GW, significantly skewing his interpretation of the study results to

21           support a higher minimum threshold. 4

16         Additionally, it presents a greater opportunity for gaming by developers. SWEPCO

4    Q.    DO YOU AGREE THAT LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS TAKING SERVICE

5          PURSUANT TO THE ES-LL CONTRACT SHOULD BE TREATED AS A

6          SEPARATE CUSTOMER CLASS?

 7   A.    SWEPCO is amenable to considering different rate designs that appropriately allocate

 8         costs to large load customers, including the possibility of creating a separate customer

 9         class or multiple customer classes at the appropriate time. However, aside from size,

10         ES-LL customers are not categorically unlike other large power customers, all of whom

11         generally have large demand requirements, high load factors, transmission-level

12         service, and the need for cost-based service under an existing large load rate

13         framework. Moreover, Mr. McGlothlin’s statement that existing Large Lighting and

14         Power Service (LLP) Transmission customers average a 54% load factor versus

15         SWEPCO’s projected 85% load factor for ES-LL customers deserves clarification.

16         Based on SWEPCO’s updated allocation factor workpaper (WP P-12) filed in response

17         to discovery in its most recent base rate case (PUCT Docket No. 58819), the LLP

18         Transmission customer class had an actual load factor of 79.4%, which is generally

19         consistent with load factors SWEPCO anticipates for the proposed large loads taking

20         service under the ES-LL Contract and would negate the need for a separate class based
